articles.title: Alligator sneaks into North Carolina bagel shop, sends owner scrambling in encounter caught on camera
articles.summary: Surveillance video captures Jesse Driscoll's stunned reaction as a 3-foot alligator slips into Bagel Dock Express in Southport, North Carolina.
articles.body: A North Carolina bagel shop owner got an unexpected scare when a 3-foot alligator wandered into his business, turning an ordinary afternoon into a wildlife encounter caught on surveillance video. The reptile entered Bagel Dock Express in Southport on Oct. 29, slipping through an open back door and making its way through the kitchen toward the front counter. Surveillance video captured owner Jesse Driscoll's startled reaction when he spotted the alligator inside the shop. Driscoll quickly backed away from the animal before calling 911. BEAR CRASHES COUPLE'S ANNIVERSARY GETAWAY, RUMMAGES THROUGH TENNESSEE TEA SHOP BEFORE JUMPING ON COUNTER The business was closed to customers at the time, and Driscoll told WWAY News that he had been distracted by workers installing a new oven when the unexpected visitor appeared. "It's just so far out of the ordinary for a bagel shop," Driscoll told the media outlet. The shop owner said he was accustomed to seeing familiar faces stop by the business, but an alligator was something he never imagined encountering. Southport police and Animal Protective Services responded to the business and removed the reptile. HUGE BULL MOOSE STUCK IN MONTANA SKATE PARK HAD TO BE TRANQUILIZED IN ORDER TO BE RESCUED The Southport Police Department confirmed the incident in a Facebook post, saying officers worked alongside Animal Protective Services Officer Ward to capture the alligator and relocate it. Bagel Dock Express also made light of the encounter in a Facebook post, joking that its reputation had apparently reached beyond its usual customers. FISHERMAN CAPTURES A CRAZY VIDEO OF AN ALLIGATOR CHASING A BEAR ACROSS A FLORIDA RIVER "Apparently, word of our fresh bagels has made its way into the swamp!" the post's caption began. "Our surprise visitor was safely escorted out by local law enforcement. No injuries, no drama… just one VERY unusual customer! Fresh bagels. Wild experiences." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The encounter was not Southport's first unusual alligator sighting this year. In April, officers helped remove a 12-foot alligator from a residential property, and another alligator was found beneath a car at a bank drive-through.

articles.title: A Scottish wildlife rescuer saved a starving badger cub trapped in a cattle trough, but officials denied his request to keep her; now he is fighting to retain the animal he says cannot survive in the wild
articles.summary: A chance encounter with a helpless animal has turned into a complicated battle over wildlife protection, rehabilitation and the limits of human
articles.body: A chance encounter with a helpless animal has turned into a complicated battle over wildlife protection, rehabilitation and the limits of human intervention. When Scottish ecologist Graeme Wilson rescued a starving badger cub from a cattle trough, he expected to nurse her back to health. Instead, the experience left him convinced that returning her to the wild could put her life in danger. Now, he is fighting for permission to give Harriet a permanent home, despite opposition from wildlife authorities.From a desperate rescue to an unusual bondAccording to the BBC, Harriet was discovered in April trapped inside a cattle trough, around 100 metres from her sett in the Scottish Borders. Wilson was called to help the young animal and took responsibility for her recovery, gradually nursing her back to health.However, her behaviour soon raised concerns about whether she could survive independently. Given her bottle feeding response and familiarity with humans, Wilson suspected Harriet was hand-reared before her rescue.As reported by The Telegraph, Wilson believes the cub has become accustomed to humans to such an extent that releasing her into the countryside could expose her to serious risks. He fears she might approach people while out walking, potentially placing herself in a dangerous situation.Why the ecologist wants to keep HarrietWilson operates GW Ecology, an independent wildlife rescue and rehabilitation service from his home in Denholm. Alongside caring for injured animals, his work involves ecological surveys to identify protected species at proposed development sites. He also organises bat walks, workshops and educational activities to encourage greater awareness of wildlife conservation.The ecologist applied to NatureScot for an educational licence that would allow him to continue caring for Harriet while helping the public understand badgers and the challenges involved in rehabilitating protected wildlife.However, the application was rejected. NatureScot suggested that Harriet should either be returned to the wild or transferred to a zoo. Wilson believes neither option would adequately address her circumstances. While a release could expose her to injury or death, he fears a conventional zoo environment would leave her isolated and distressed.Wildlife experts raise concernsThe disagreement has brought wider questions about the responsibilities involved in wildlife rehabilitation into focus. The BBC reported that the British Wildlife Rehabilitation Council has stressed the specialist nature of caring for wild animals.Paul Reynolds, who chairs the organisation, has highlighted the importance of suitable facilities, species-specific care, veterinary supervision and an understanding of an animal's natural behaviour. The council also distinguishes responsible rehabilitation from keeping wild animals permanently in captivity for educational or personal purposes.According to The Telegraph, the organisation maintains that an animal becoming accustomed to human contact should not automatically be considered grounds for permanent captivity.Harriet's future remains uncertainNatureScot has indicated that discussions with Wilson and other relevant organisations are continuing in an effort to find a practical resolution. The authority has emphasised that Harriet's welfare remains central to its decision-making process. Police Scotland has also been made aware of the situation.Meanwhile, the Scottish SPCA advises people who encounter sick or injured badgers to contact its rescue officers rather than attempting to handle the animals themselves. Young cubs found away from their setts may need help, and frightened or injured badgers may attack.Wilson still wants a safe future for Harriet. Whether that means an exception to the usual rules or another arrangement, the case highlights the difficult balance between individual animal welfare and the principles of wildlife conservation.Images Courtesy: istock and BBCYou use AI every day. articles.title: 17 years after Fort Hood massacre, victims' families grapple with gunman's looming execution
articles.summary: Three families of the 2009 Fort Hood shooting victims share how they've navigated grief as Nidal Hasan's firing squad execution nears on Dec. 3.
articles.body: Seventeen years have passed since an Army psychiatrist opened fire at Fort Hood, killing 13 people in 2009. Since then, families of three of the fallen have learned to navigate life without their loved ones, finding strength in the values and lessons their father, daughter and spouse left behind. "It builds character, kid," is a phrase Keely Cahill Vanacker remembers her father, Michael Cahill, saying, always with a playful punch to the arm, throughout her teenage years whenever she was upset. Cahill served in the Army National Guard for 23 years as an infantryman before earning a bachelor’s degree in psychology and training to become a physician assistant (PA), providing medical care to soldiers. "My dad really valued people, and he touched a lot of lives," Vanacker said. TRUMP CLEARS WAY FOR FORT HOOD TERRORIST TO FACE ARMY FIRING SQUAD NEARLY 17 YEARS AFTER MASSACRE Growing up in a military family, living all across the country, Vanacker saw Cahill demonstrate the value of treating others with humanity and fairness as he practiced medicine. "If you were somebody living in a rural Texas post and struggling to even pay for your asthma medication, my dad would find places for you to get your medication," she said. For Cahill, serving people was a calling; and it did not end when he hung up his helmet. After retiring from the military, he continued to serve as a civilian PA at Fort Hood. As for Amy Krueger, her call to serve came in the aftermath of the Sept. 11, 2001, terror attacks. 2001 turning point "I’m going in." Those are the words Amy told her mother, Jeri Krueger, on the afternoon of Sept. 11. At the time, Amy was a student at the University of Wisconsin-Green Bay, Sheboygan Campus. "Going in?" Krueger recalled asking her daughter. "I'm joining the Army, mom." Krueger was skeptical that her daughter could make a difference in the fight against terrorism. "Oh, Amy, you can't take on bin Laden all by yourself," Krueger told her daughter. "Watch me," Amy replied. The next day, Amy sat in a recruiter's office and would go on to become Staff Sgt. Amy Krueger. "When Amy said she was going to do something, she did it," Krueger said. After Amy's first deployment to Afghanistan in 2003 at Bagram Airfield, she returned home and continued her education as a mental health specialist in the Army and completed Emergency Medical Technician (EMT) and Certified Nursing Assistant (CNA) programs while continuing her education in psychology. "She wanted to help people get through things," Krueger said. "Psychology was definitely something she would've been great at." In 2008, Amy volunteered for another tour in Afghanistan. Between deployments, she was welcomed home by friends and family members. Even while at home, her commitment to service was still at the forefront of her mind. Krueger had been at work when Amy texted her a picture of a new tattoo she had gotten, which took hours to complete. "I said, ‘I don't like it,’" Krueger recalled. Amy asked what her mother meant, thinking she was receiving the typical parental disapproval of new ink. Krueger explained it wasn't necessarily the tattoo itself she disliked, but what it said. "I feel like it's a bad omen," Krueger had told her daughter. Amy brushed her mother's worries off with a chuckle. The tattoo depicted the American flag, draped across her back, alongside a firearm and soldier’s hat. It read: "All gave some. Some gave all. Sacrifice." Krueger knew her daughter was determined to continue serving. However, after seeing the new tattoo, Krueger said she couldn't shake the ominous feeling it gave her. "I always thought she had a feeling that she might not come back," Krueger said. "That tattoo kind of says that. I think that she was prepared to fight, to do what she needed to do, and didn't know if she'd be coming back." By October 2009, Amy was sent to Fort Hood to prepare for a deployment in December, a deployment she never made. She was not alone in arriving at Fort Hood with plans for a deployment ahead. Staff Sgt. Justin DeCrow was also preparing to deploy, this time to Iraq, when he reported to Fort Hood. SON WHO LOST FATHER IN 9/11 ATTACKS SHARES POWERFUL LESSONS 25 YEARS LATER: ‘I’M STILL HERE’ Justin DeCrow From an early age, Justin knew he wanted to join the Army, being influenced by his father, Daniel J. DeCrow, who served in the Vietnam War. He then went on to become a satellite communication instructor, where he was known for his work ethic and uplifting others. "His positive attitude and humor helped others get through tough times," said Justin's wife, Marikay DeCrow. When fellow soldiers struggled, Justin stayed to help, teach, support and encourage them. For him, failure was not an option. That same warmth carried into his personal life. Justin and Marikay had known each other since childhood, as he was friends with her brother. It wasn’t until she asked him to her senior prom that they solidified feelings for one another and became inseparable. "From that time on, we were together," said Marikay. "When he would look at me, all I saw was the love he had for me. I couldn't imagine my life without him." When they had their daughter Kylah, Justin wasn’t able to return home and meet his daughter for the first time until she was six weeks old. Justin had learned of his daughter Kylah’s birth 24 hours after the fact, when he was finally able to call Marikay at the hospital. "He was ecstatic to have a daughter," she said. "We had maybe a phone call for five minutes once a day." The phone calls were a beacon of hope, offering Marikay a few precious moments of connection with Justin while they were apart. The hardship continued when Justin attended Advanced Individual Training (AIT) in South Carolina. Marikay recounted traveling back and forth every other weekend to keep the family in contact. "Sometimes we only had a day, sometimes he was allowed to stay the night with us," said Marikay. "Every trip meant so much to him and us. He spent every minute he could holding Kylah. Leaving him each time was incredibly difficult." As Kylah grew up, he was always there for her. To this day, Kylah reflects the values of her father. "I see so much of Justin in Kylah," said Marikay. "She is witty and funny, and cares so much about those around her." Neither of them knew then how precious those days would become, the last they’d have before he headed to Fort Hood. Nov. 5, 2009 It was a Thursday at Fort Hood’s Soldier Readiness Processing Center when U.S. Army major and psychiatrist Nidal Hasan opened fire, killing 13 people and leaving 31 wounded. Hasan had been motivated by Islamic extremism and had negative views on America’s involvement in Afghanistan and Iraq. Among those 13 were Retired Chief Warrant Officer 2 Michael Cahill, Staff Sgt. Krueger and Staff Sgt. Justin DeCrow, three people whose lives were defined by their service, values and families. For the families, the attack was the start of a new struggle: trying to understand what happened and how they spent their final moments. Putting back broken pieces After the shooting, piecing together the fragments of that day was difficult for Vanacker. Witnesses were hospitalized with injuries or scattered across the country, and many of Cahill’s colleagues had not seen what he did in his final moments. Vanacker didn’t get a solid first description until a memorial, when she was approached by a soldier who had shared a cubicle with Cahill. He described it as any other workday until he heard gunfire down the hall. "And all of a sudden, your dad just got up, and then he was gone," she recalled him saying. The uncertainty that followed stretched on for nearly a year as she waited to learn what had happened to her father. "I was just trying to figure out what had happened and if he was shot trying to help somebody," she recalled. "Was it that sort of thing? It leaves things unanswered for a while, and you have this weird waiting game." When the pretrial proceedings began, she learned that Cahill had emerged from the examination room before picking up a chair by its legs and charging at Hasan, an act of courage that reflected "character," what he'd spent a lifetime instilling in his children. In August 2013, Hasan was convicted on all 42 counts by a military jury that then unanimously agreed to give Hasan the death penalty. For 13 years, Hasan has been on the military's death row. In 2015, after Congress expanded eligibility for the Purple Heart, military victims of the massacre received Purple Hearts, while eligible civilian victims, including Cahill, received the Secretary of Defense Medal for the Defense of Freedom. Hasan's long-awaited fate On Oct. 2, President Donald Trump approved the sentence of Hasan, and acting Army Secretary Adam Telle directed that the execution be carried out by firing squad on Dec. 3. Hasan's execution would be the U.S. military's first execution since 1961 and its first by firing squad since 1945. "When I received the email that President Trump signed the execution order, I felt a kind of relief come over me, all I could do was cry," said Marikay. "I have been waiting for 17 years to hear this." Although the execution method has been questioned by some, Marikay said the method does not matter as long as Hasan faces his end. "He deserves the death penalty, this is justice," said Marikay. "This man destroyed our lives. Justin never got to watch Kylah grow up, graduate, walk her down the aisle, hold his beautiful granddaughters ... We were supposed to grow old together." Vanacker and Krueger said they did not need Hasan's execution for closure. "He was already dead to me, and I did not think about him. So having an execution is not something I personally needed for my own closure," Vanacker said. Krueger expressed a similar sentiment. "I do not give him any thought ever. He died a long time ago," she said. Vanacker and Krueger also bring up another point being the execution may be giving into Hasan’s desires. "He wanted to be a martyr, and that didn't happen," said Krueger. "So when this happens, does that fulfill his desires?" 9/11 SENT THEM TO WAR. 25 YEARS LATER, VETERANS GRAPPLE WITH WHAT FOLLOWED "He did that shooting, and he did it in a way where he wanted that attention, and he wanted to become a martyr, and we have just played right into his hands," said Vanacker. The debate over Hasan’s execution took a turn when War Secretary Pete Hegseth said the administration planned to livestream the event. "We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it in public, because people need to understand that there are serious consequences for these types of things," Hegseth said. The families said it was the first time hearing of the livestream plan. "It feels a little bit like a slap in the face, disrespectful," said Krueger. "I'm sure he didn't intend it but … there should have been somebody that said, 'whoa, wait a minute. There are families that are going to be affected by this.'" Before Trump announced the cancellation of the planned livestream via Truth Social, Vanacker expressed concern that the administration's handling of the execution could have jeopardized it. "Hegseth's obsession with barbaric optics probably put this execution in danger," Vanacker said. "Our tragedy is not your entertainment." She called on Congress to ban livestreamed executions in the military using the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA). "I hope they put in the NDAA just banning it outright," she said. "That it can never be considered and not an option ever, so it never comes up again. Livestreaming an execution should never be an option." After the planned livestream was canceled, Krueger was relieved. "I'm so, so grateful that President Trump took it down, so that's a good thing," Krueger said. Victims’ families are allowed to witness Hasan’s execution and Marikay has no doubt what she will be doing on Dec. 3. "The date it was announced, I knew I would be heading to Fort Hood one last time," Marikay said. "This is closure. I'm ready for it to be over." Grieving together Nov. 5 remains a personal day for the families. For them, this day goes beyond Hasan, focusing on the ones they lost. Krueger remembers her daughter as vivacious and strong, someone who had a way of passing that strength on to others. Today, that same strength continues to carry her mother and how she thinks about what happened. "I hate the idealism that made him do what he did," Krueger said. "But do I hate him? He’s a human being that was swayed by the beliefs of his leaders and had the free will to carry out a devastating, destructive event." To continue Amy’s legacy, they have an annual event to raise money for the scholarship in her honor at the local high school. And just like her daughter, they raise money in a fun way: a bar crawl called Krueg’s Crawl. "It's a bar crawl, and there's prizes, and so it's fun," said Krueger. This year's event took place on Halloween and consisted of a costume contest, keeping the fun alive in her memory. When Nov. 5 hits, the family remains intimate. "We typically do the same thing," Krueger said. "We get together, we go to the cemetery, we talk about her, we remember her, and this year we're doing that as well." Vanacker and her family revisit their traditions by visiting her father. "We go, and we leave flowers, and we have a remembrance," she said. What got her through the first anniversary was her father's four-word sentiment, the same words Cahill had comforted her with through childhood: "It builds character, kid." "I think this year's a little bit different," Vanacker said. "I think with all the other distractions around, it honestly makes it a little harder. There's a lot more emotions pulling this year." Although the media attention surrounding the case has brought back emotions for families, the tragedy and hardship these families faced has brought them together. "We've become like a family," Krueger said. "There was one year and there was a 10-year anniversary to see them and to be with them, that's huge for me." articles.title: Cetirizine: Kenyan pharmacists warn against using allergy drug for vaginal tightening
articles.summary: Women who have already tried inserting the tablets are advised to stop and seek medical attention if needed.
articles.body:
Kenyan pharmacists have warned women against inserting allergy tablets into their vaginas in an attempt to make them tighter, following the spread of potentially dangerous medical advice on social media.

The warning follows a wave of social media posts promoting cetirizine - a widely available oral antihistamine used to treat allergies - as a way of tightening the vagina, supposedly to enhance sexual pleasure.

Although antihistamines can sometimes cause dryness as a side effect, experts say this does not strengthen vaginal muscles.

"Dryness is not tightness... instead, it may increase friction, discomfort, and the risk of tissue injury," the Pharmaceutical Society of Kenya (PSK) said.

"Inserting oral tablets is unsafe. Cetirizine tablets are made to be swallowed. Their ingredients have not been tested on delicate vaginal tissue," it added.

Cetirizine is commonly used to relieve symptoms such as sneezing, a runny nose, itchy eyes and skin reactions, including hives.

The controversy began earlier this week when posts circulated on TikTok claiming that cetirizine could reduce vaginal moisture and create a sensation of tightness during sex.

This sparked widespread debate, with some users promoting the practice while others questioned its safety.

There have also been local media reports of the price of the drug rising and increased demand in some pharmacies, especially in the capital, Nairobi.

"Cetirizine is an allergy medicine, taken by mouth. It is not approved or tested for any other purpose, and definitely not for vaginal use," the PSK, a professional body representing pharmacists in Kenya, said in a statement issued on Thursday.

"If you have already tried it. Stop. See a doctor if you have pain, bleeding, burning, itching, unusual discharge, or fever," it advised.

The society also urged social media influencers and content creators to take care when sharing health information, saying that unverified claims could put people's health at risk.

The warning comes a day after Kenya's health ministry expressed concern about the trend.

Ouma Oluga, a senior health official, said some social media users appeared to be treating the medical advice from experts as a joke, without considering the possible consequences.

He suggested that the authorities could introduce a system to track the distribution and purchase of medicines to help identify possible misuse.

However, no formal decision has been announced on such a initiative.

The PSK said it was aware of reports of increased demand for cetirizine, rising prices and shortages at some pharmacies.

It urged retailers not to exploit the trend, warning that people who genuinely needed the medicine for allergies could struggle to obtain it.

It went on to encourage its members not to knowingly dispense medicines that would be misused - and report any side affects to the health authorities of those that had been.

The PSK ended its statement by saying that unverified online trends should never trump what the experts say: "Check with a pharmacist before using any medicine for a purpose it was not made for.

"Do not rely on social media for medical advice."

articles.title: Hundreds of thousands march in France as protesters clash with police
articles.summary: France is bracing for what could be its biggest demonstrations in years with between 500,000 and 700,000 protesters. Follow for the latest updates.
articles.body:
• General strike : Riot police have fired tear gas and charged a group of protesters in Lyon in central France while scuffles have broken out in the western city of Nantes, as demonstrations take place across the country. Around 270,000 people were taking part in nearly 200 demonstrations across France – not including Paris.

• Widespread disruptions : The strike is organized by L’intersyndicale, the group that represents all of France’s main trade unions. Education, health care, public transportation and other sectors are likely to be impacted with many services closed for the day. But the strikes go beyond the public sector with many employees of private companies planning to join in.

• Europe discontent : Anti-government protests have swept across the continent in recent weeks. In Greece , students and teachers gathered in central Athens to stress the importance of free public education and protest the rising housing and food costs affecting students, as marches were getting underway in France on Thursday.

Almost 600,000 protesters are on the streets of France today, the country’s interior ministry has just estimated, making Thursday the biggest day of protests since this current wave of unrest began in September.

Earlier today, at 1 p.m. local time (7 a.m. ET), the ministry had estimated that 270,000 people were protesting but that number excluded Paris, where a march began this afternoon.

The ministry is expected to release its final figures later today but, as of now, its current estimates indicate that these demonstrations are not quite as big as the 2023 pension reform protests.

French education minister Édouard Geffray has condemned what he said was a “deliberate act of arson” at a school near the city of Toulouse in southern France.

The minister thanked firefighters and law enforcement officials for helping to “limit the damage” cause by the flames.

“This deliberate act of arson could have had tragic consequences for human life. I condemn it in the strongest possible terms and call on everyone to condemn it unequivocally,” he added, while vowing to hold those responsible to account.

Earlier, France’s interior ministry said the blaze started after fireworks were directed at an office hosting the school’s student services.

Authorities in Rennes said they arrested “several dozen” masked individuals who vandalized a hotel, threw objects at police and “violently attacked” union members who were protesting earlier today.

Photos taken by local media show that vandals smashed the hotel’s glass doors and painted graffiti on windows.

Some masked individuals also tried to erect barricades to block some of the city’s roads, lit fires in garbage bins, and threw heavy pétanque balls – used in a popular French game – at police, authorities added.

Despite violent clashes like this, however, the protests today have largely been peaceful even as they have been attended by hundreds of thousands of people.

As today’s march in Paris got underway, the trade unions were in a jubilant mood. Music blared out as the crowd, dominated by left-wing groups, sang and chanted slogans against the government and the far-right.

A police helicopter buzzed above, but in the confines of the avenue we were walking down, there was little sense of the heavy police presence around the protest.

In the distance, the soaring statue of Marianne – the national symbol of France – got smaller and smaller as the march inched its way forward.

The protest route is packed. The movement of the crowd has been brought to a near standstill at points by the sheer quantity of people.

Later, several protesters were seen lying on the ground being treated by street medics, with blood flowing from the head of an older man. A bystander said the man was struck by police, but an officer at the scene said they were unaware of any incident.

At one point, protesters scattered as tear gas was deployed by police, followed by mass cries of “everyone hates the police.”

The mood of the crowd has lost its upbeat feel.

Several of France’s biggest unions, representing everyone from students, teachers and postal workers to doctors, pharmacists and transport workers, have called for a nationwide strike. So, how is that affecting these essential services?

Schools: About 13% of all school staff are participating in the strikes, France’s education ministry estimates, including 16% of all teachers. Around 19% of schools and 18% of colleges across France are affected by the strike.

Universities: About one in three of France’s higher education are “disrupted” because of the strikes and protests, the government told CNN.

Hospitals: Very few public hospital staff – only about 4% of the workforce – are participating in the strike, France’s healthcare ministry told CNN. “No significant disruption to healthcare services has been reported,” the ministry added. Two of France’s main unions representing both public and private healthcare workers had called on them to strike, citing the high cost of living and the deterioriation of public services.

Transport: Four in 10 of today’s scheduled trains have been canceled, though a handful of those cancelations are due to other factors like unavailable equipment, according to tracking website Trayn.

The labor unions that have called today’s demonstrations in France are demanding higher wages and pensions. In particular, the largest of the unions – the CGT – says the minimum wage needs to be increased immediately by 10%.

Last month, the CGT claimed there had been a big increase in the number of professions paying some employees less than the minimum wage. Another union - the CFDT – is demanding a 100 euro increase in the minimum monthly wage, about 7%.

Maud Millier, a CGT official in Lyon, said that the government’s announced minimum wage increase, from November 1, amounts to just €15 for someone earning the minimum wage, which she said was nowhere near enough given rising fuel and food prices.

Employers’ groups have warned that such increases would harm competitiveness and threaten employment.

Other groups involved in the protests have different demands. Students’ groups are demanding an increase of more than $10 billion in the education budget, as well as $1.5 billion investment in school infrastructure and 250,000 additional university places.

The Gilets Jaunes or Yellow Vests – a radical movement that first emerged eight years ago – is demanding the departure of President Emmanuel Macron and his government, and a new constitutional process. It also protests economic inequality but has no formal leadership.

Police have said that “Black Bloc” protesters are on the streets today – agitators accused by French authorities of provoking violence towards the end of largely peaceful demonstrations in recent weeks.

Black Bloc protesters usually wear matching or similar black clothing, face masks and hoods during protests to hide their identity. But it’s not an organization with formal leadership; rather it’s a set of protest tactics. They first appeared in Germany in the 1980s and are mostly associated with anarchist and anti-capitalist movements. These methods gained prominence in France during the 2016 labor protests before spreading further during the Yellow Vest movement.

One Black Bloc tactic involves small, highly mobile groups breaking away from the main march, forcing police to spread their forces thin, making it harder for them to respond in a coordinated way.

That was on display last month when a group of protesters attempted to reach the Elysee Palace, drawing riot police away from the October 17 demonstration. The maneuver worked. Police resources were stretched, and it contributed to officers being overwhelmed that day.

Police have clashed with demonstrators in the city of Lyon in central France. Riot police fired tear gas ​and charged a group of protesters, many of them masked, in scenes broadcast by CNN affiliate BFMTV. Some of the protesters were throwing objects towards the police, while a car was also set on fire.

There are 800 “Black Bloc” protesters present in the city, according to police.

Thousands of people are marching through central Lyon despite public transport workers being on strike, according to Maud Millier, regional secretary of the main labor union, the CGT.

There have also been scuffles in the city of Nantes in western France, where footage on BFMTV showed police firing tear gas as a tractor made its way through the city, surrounded by protesters.

The outlet also reported that a high school near the city of Toulouse was set ‌on fire on Thursday morning.

At 1 p.m. local time (7 a.m. ET), 270,000 people were taking part in nearly 200 demonstrations across France in the nationwide day of action organized by labor unions, according to the Interior Ministry.

That total excluded the capital, Paris, where a march is due to get underway shortly, but is higher than the number involved in protests outside Paris last weekend.

“The marches are generally proceeding smoothly, and some are still ongoing. However, tensions have been reported in Lyon, where several hundred individuals have formed a black bloc,” the Interior ministry said. The “black bloc” refers to masked protestors.

“In Nantes, initial incidents have been reported as the march disperses,” the ministry said, while in Paris “numerous unauthorized marches are being systematically monitored and dispersed by police on public roads.”

Near Toulouse, a fire broke out on the grounds of a school after incendiary devices were thrown, the ministry said.

“Law enforcement remains heavily mobilized for the afternoon demonstrations to contain violent groups, prevent unrest and intervene whenever necessary to protect people, secure the marches and safeguard public buildings.”

Meanwhile in Greece, students and teachers have gathered in central Athens to stress the importance of free public education and protest the rising housing and food costs affecting students.

They held banners with painted-on phrases like “free and public education, safe facilities, that is what is right for students” according to Reuters, and forced roads in central Athens to close, the country’s national broadcaster ERT said.

“We demand dignified salaries, safe buildings, schools that educate all our students regardless of economic background, origin or gender,” Andreas Kargopoulous, president of a high school teachers union, told Reuters.

“We find the situation at the schools unacceptable, in terms of the facilities and the very nature of the schooling provided, which has been transformed into an exorbitantly expensive examination center.”

The Eiffel Tower, which attracts 7 million visitors a year, is closed today due to the national strike organized by French unions.

The 330-meter (1,083-foot) historic landmark has shut its doors before due to industrial action, including earlier this year during a strike by staff members. It was also closed in 2025 amid a searing heatwave .

Today’s general strike and protests have been organized by L’intersyndicale, the group that represents all of France’s main trade unions.

Education, health care, public transportation and other sectors are expected to be impacted, with many services shut for the day. But the strikes go beyond the public sector as employees of private companies are also joining in.

Other groups likely to be in attendance include students, climate activists and the Yellow Vests, the grassroots citizens’ movement established in 2018, as well as some allegedly extremist groups.

Some high street businesses in the French capital boarded up their stores ahead of today’s demonstrations, as Parisians braced for another round of protests over the cost of living and other grievances.

Meanwhile, local police have been deployed to train stations across the city, with searches being carried out to confiscate dangerous items.

“No equipment intended for committing acts of violence should reach the gathering places,” police posted on X.

French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said Wednesday that no level of disorder would be tolerated and arrests would be made if necessary.

He added that routes have been agreed between authorities and trade unions in almost all cities where protests are expected, but some disagreements remain.

CNN’s Lucie Lepellec and Pierre Bairin contributed reporting.

The US embassy in France has warned of possible rail, metro, road and flight disruption as a result of today’s demonstrations, as well as the potential closure of hospitals and banks.

In the statement, the embassy set out several anticipated impacts including “possible closures or reduced services in Paris and across France” affecting schools, hospitals, banks and government offices.

It also advised US citizens to avoid areas where demonstrations or large gatherings were due to take place and “plan alternative routes and allow extra travel time for travel.”

France is not the only European country seeing angry anti-government protests.

Belgium, Germany, Spain, Italy, Portugal and Albania have all seen unrest in recent weeks. Each country has its own unique problems which sparked their protests, but the economy is a key factor in all of them.

In Germany, a new youth-led movement dubbed “Gen Z has got this!” protested last weekend against the high cost of living, underfunded schools and universities, environmental concerns and a potential reintroduction of mandatory military service . While many of the protests were peaceful, water cannons and riot police were deployed in Cologne and Hamburg.

In Albania, anti-corruption protests were triggered by a proposed luxury resort project from Ivanka Trump and her husband Jared Kushner. In Italy, rising fuel prices first forced people into the streets, while in Portugal, the issue of affordable housing was initially the main driver.

In Spain, the Ceuta migration crisis and the nationwide lack of affordable housing are among the main issues on protesters’ minds.

Underneath this discontent across the continent lie similar themes: the poor state of the economy, rising cost of living and dissatisfaction with governments’ responses to these problems.

The protests in France come against the backdrop of a shaky economy, with the country’s growth lagging behind other EU members and its debt drawing scrutiny from credit rating agencies.

The French economy is perilously close to going into recession after shrinking 0.1% in the third quarter of the year. Consumer demand is weak, investment in manufacturing shrinking and its farming sector was hurt by a hot, dry summer.

The Bank of France is likely going to have to lower its already anemic forecast of 0.4% growth for 2026, Governor Emmanuel Moulin said this week.

“Unfortunately, I think it’s a bit too optimistic,” he said Tuesday.

France’s sovereign debt stands at $4 trillion, and it’s having to offer bonds at higher returns to attract buyers. This only increases the amount of interest the country must pay in coming years.

Fitch Ratings marked France’s credit score down at the end of October, saying it “reflects a deterioration since our August 2026 review comprising weaker growth, higher borrowing costs and a wider deficit.”

“These worsen debt dynamics from an already weak starting point,” Fitch added.

Successive governments have done little to rein in welfare payments beyond trying to raise the retirement age in 2023. France’s National Assembly has since suspended a reform that would have raised the retirement age from 62 to 64 for most workers until the 2027 presidential election.

articles.title: Palantir harvests battlefield data that Ukraine pays for ‘with blood’
articles.summary: The US company is using Kyiv’s unique war data to train its controversial technologies.
articles.body:
Months into Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine , Palantir’s CEO Alex Karp became the first chief of a major Western Big Tech company to personally visit Kyiv.

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in June 2022 that he was “delighted” to receive the support of such a company in the fight against Russia “on the digital front line”.

The Florida-based software development firm’s partnership has paid off.

Ukraine has since become the first nation in modern history to systematically collect battlefield data, a crucial asset for training military artificial intelligence (AI) to recognise patterns and make predictions.

The trove of real-world combat data obtained from video and sensor feeds over four years of conflict is helping Ukraine monitor, predict and respond to Russian attacks with the help of Palantir’s products.

Yet observers say the data is also boosting the capabilities of the United States corporation whose technologies are implicated in human rights abuses, including in Israel’s genocide in Gaza , raising questions about the growing leverage that private tech corporations are acquiring over sovereign states.

Palantir was founded in the aftermath of the 2001 attack on New York’s World Trade Center to help the US defence industry build a single data environment from which to monitor and respond to incoming threats.

To reflect such a mission, the company was named after a stone in JRR Tolkien’s The Lord of the Rings that grants powers that border on omniscience.

Yasir Atalan, deputy director of the Futures Lab at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), said Palantir makes “different forms of data talk to each other”.

In the military context, data from missiles, radars, the automatic identification system (AIS) and open sources is gathered on one screen, offering a “larger view of the battlefield”, Atalan said.

Similar solutions are available to governments for civil purposes, including border control, health services, tax and revenue – and mass surveillance.

With more data, systems use statistical learning to recognise patterns to make accurate predictions, enabling military systems to make split-second, automated tactical decisions.

Under this premise, large datasets based on real-life scenarios are coveted by companies aiming to outperform their competitors.

“Good battlefield data is extremely rare and hard to come by,” Elke Schwarz, a lecturer focusing on digital technologies at Queen Mary University of London, told Al Jazeera. Because of its scarcity, “those with access to [it] have a strategic advantage”.

Data originating from Ukraine may not be directly applicable to another conflict but is still crucial for training, Schwarz said.

“Building a system that correctly identifies a tank, for instance, requires a large volume of tank images, ideally in all kinds of weather conditions,” she explained.

Similarly, large volumes of behavioural data – information on how people react to a given scenario – are key in tracking, profiling and predicting human activity in mass surveillance systems.

The pinnacle of the collaboration between Palantir and Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence came in January with the launch of a specialised software platform, the Brave1 Dataroom, which uses battlefield data to train artificial intelligence for military applications.

But prominent figures in Ukraine’s defence sector have questioned their government’s decision to share the country’s valuable asset with a private tech company under undisclosed terms.

“Ukraine has something that no other country in the world has,” Valerii Markus, a serviceman and former chief sergeant, wrote on Facebook. “We are paying with blood for data that someone else can convert into capital, international influence, and big money.”

The company maintains it does not acquire customer data.

In an emailed statement to Al Jazeera, it said that “customers own and control their data”.

Palantir’s software helps them “integrate and analyse their existing data sets,” the company said, adding: “Palantir never uses or retains customer data for its own purposes.”

Schwarz, at Queen Mary University London, said Palantir does not need to possess the data to benefit from it. “Rather, it works with the data that is made available,” she said.

Palantir’s technologies, contracted by private clients and government agencies around the world, are known to have been implicated in human rights abuses.

Its core software platforms, ICM and FALCON, facilitated the administration of US President Donald Trump in detaining and deporting thousands of people, including asylum seekers, since January 2025. Amnesty International found the company aggregated massive amounts of data, built detailed individual profiles to track migrants and asylum seekers and assisted with deportations, contrary to its obligations to avoid causing or contributing to human rights abuses under international law.

The company has also assisted Israel in its war in Gaza, which a United Nations inquiry found bears the hallmarks of genocide .

Last year, UN Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese found “reasonable grounds” to believe Palantir provided AI platforms used for battlefield data integration and automated decision-making in the war that has killed more than 74,500 Palestinians since October 2023.

In the United Kingdom, the National Health Service (NHS), police, military and local councils all signed multimillion-pound contracts with Palantir to integrate user data, but the agreements have been met with public backlash.

Nonprofit organisation Corporate Accountability launched a campaign against the 330-million-pound ($440m) contract between the NHS and Palantir to provide a new data platform. The watchdog warned the company is “at the heart of the dystopian marriage of Big Tech, the surveillance and detention industry, and rising fascism”.

Palantir in April published a 22-point summary of Karp’s coauthored book on X, which was widely criticised for promoting an authoritarian, antidemocratic worldview by questioning the efficacy of liberal democracy and arguing that some cultures produce vital advances while others are regressive.

Fatimah Shaikh, Corporate Accountability’s deputy campaigns director, said, “Palantir is not a corporation we can trust” to hold British citizens’ sensitive personal information.

“We should all be able to get medical care without fearing for our safety or privacy,” she told Al Jazeera.

Ilia Siatitsa, senior legal officer at Privacy International in the UK, said tech companies like Palantir blur the line between military and civil applications. They are also opaque about how they use customers’ data by virtue of their involvement in national security, she added.

Siatitsa argued the company could potentially use personal information to train its products – including those with a military application – without explicit consent from the users.

“If my data is going to be feeding into a war machine, I want to know about it,” she said. “I need to have the choice, not only [as a matter of] privacy, but also from an ethical point of view.”

In June, Britain announced it was reviewing the NHS’s data contract with Palantir after parliamentary pressure.

Private tech companies are supporting military and civil infrastructure, to the point where governments may become reliant on them to conduct military operations or run national services, experts say.

Anna Nadibaidze, researcher at the Center for War Studies at the University of Southern Denmark, said the balance of power has been shifting.

“We’re used to state armies, nations’ armies being the main players,” Nadibaidze said, adding that now those players are reliant on products supplied by the private sector. “So what if they choose to not supply this infrastructure any more?”

She argued Elon Musk’s SpaceX offered a valid example.

Ukraine has come to rely heavily on the company’s Starlink satellites for communications on the battlefield and effective warfare, but in late September 2022, during a pivotal push by Ukraine to retake Kherson from Russia, the tech billionaire suddenly provoked a communications blackout.

Amid tensions between Washington and Europe, several countries are now refraining from using Palantir’s products. France’s Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu in June said domestic intelligence services would ditch Palantir’s products in an effort to avoid “strategic dependency”. Germany’s military also said it would no longer use the company’s products.

Spanish publication El Confidencial revealed in July that Spanish authorities quietly instructed state-backed companies to avoid signing new contracts with Palantir, citing concerns that sensitive national security information could be exposed.

Palantir’s reliability as a partner has also been called into question in Ukraine after the company finalised in September a strategic partnership with Nebius, a Dutch company founded as an offshoot of Russian technology giant Yandex .

Denys Shtilerman, chief designer and co-owner of Fire Point, a Ukrainian defence-tech company that develops and produces UAV and missile systems, said “the very same Palantir that works with Ukrainian combat data” had struck a deal with Yandex cofounder Arkady Volozh.

Volozh’s description of Russia’s war as “barbaric” has not eased Shtilerman’s concerns.

“Our combat data is not free raw material for Western technology corporations. It is a strategic asset of the state,” he wrote on X in a response to Kyiv’s collaboration with Palantir.

“Ukraine has paid for it with blood. We have no right to simply hand over the most valuable asset we possess.”

articles.title: An Iowa man lost $700,000 in a vacation-rental investment he believed was a Ponzi scheme; after divorce, a court upheld his wife's $351,446 property payment
articles.summary: Iowa divorce, Ponzi scheme investment loss, equalisation payment, a Lee County husband who lost $700,000 in a vacation-rental company must pay his former
articles.body: Iowa divorce, Ponzi scheme investment loss, equalisation payment, a Lee County husband who lost $700,000 in a vacation-rental company must pay his former wife $351,446 to balance their property division. The Court of Appeals of Iowa upheld that order on 4 November 2026, after a marriage lasting nearly seven years. Todd Schneider appealed the divorce decree, disputing how the trial court calculated his income, valued his rental properties and classic cars, and treated assets he owned before the marriage. Without the payment, his former wife, Julie Schneider, would have been left with a tiny net share of the couple’s property.How a vacation-rental investment collapse and a short marriage ended up before Iowa appeals judgesAccording to the Court of Appeals of Iowa, Todd and Julie Schneider became engaged in January 2013 and married in July 2017, when he was 54 and she was 35. Both had been married before. Todd had three children from his first marriage and adopted Julie’s daughter in 2018. All the children are now adults, so custody was not in dispute.Todd entered the marriage with significant wealth, built mainly on owning, running and managing rental properties. Farming on rented land and a small parcel of his own added a smaller share of his income. Julie, a licensed massage therapist, had run her own practice in Illinois before opening another in a building Todd owned, and she also helped with his rental business.Near the end of 2022, Todd suffered a heavy financial blow. Over the previous couple of years, he had invested in a vacation-rental company that went under, and he came to see it as essentially a Ponzi scheme. He expected to recover none of the money and still carried an outstanding loan of nearly $180,000.The marriage deteriorated at the same time. Julie moved out in February 2023, and Todd petitioned for divorce a few months later. A one-day trial before a judge, without a jury, took place in May 2024. Todd then appealed, and a three-judge panel considered the case without oral argument.Why judges cut the husband’s income to $110,000 but refused to touch the spousal support orderThe trial court had put Todd’s yearly income at $153,500, relying mainly on an undated, handwritten note in which he projected retirement income of $183,500 before a $30,000 withdrawal from an individual retirement account was deducted. Todd argued his real income was $73,000, the average of the rental and farm income on his tax returns.The appeals judges agreed the note was not the best evidence, since he most likely wrote it in or before January 2022, more than two years before trial. They also refused to accept his lower figure. Tax returns are usually strong evidence, they explained, but a self-employed person’s taxable income does not always show the money actually available to spend.Several findings pushed the figure upwards. Todd reported nearly $28,000 in dividend income on his 2023 return that seemed likely to continue. He also claimed about $28,000 in depreciation that year, an accounting entry rather than cash spent. His business and personal money were intermingled, which suggested some expenses were overstated.His lifestyle pointed the same way. His 2023 returns showed gambling winnings and losses of $192,672, and bank records showed repeated large cash withdrawals at casinos. He spent three winter months in Florida and kept buying classic cars. The panel settled on $110,000.That lower figure did not change the spousal support order of $2,000 a month. Todd made no argument for how the amount should be adjusted, and the judges said they would not construct his case for him. They added that Julie’s income of roughly $24,000 left her unable to sustain her accustomed lifestyle, and that the support can end as soon as the property payment is made and runs for 24 months at most.Why premarital property still counted and how judges valued a rental property, house and carsTodd argued that assets he bought before the marriage should be treated as nonmarital and kept out of the division. The judges rejected that. Iowa law directs courts to divide all property equitably, excluding only inheritances and gifts, and that includes property a spouse owned before the wedding. Premarital ownership can be weighed as a factor, but it does not shield an asset automatically. For property that grew in value during the marriage, courts give special weight to each spouse’s tangible contributions, whether the growth came from luck or effort, and how long the marriage lasted.Todd then challenged three valuations. He said the trial court overstated the appreciation of a rental property on Avenue H by $20,000. The court had measured the gain from the 2017 assessed value of $110,390 to the agreed 2024 value of $209,040, giving $98,650. Todd wanted a 2009 appraisal of $131,000 used as the starting point. The appeals court said using assessed values consistently made sense.He also claimed the marital home, valued at $723,370 under an agreement the couple filed the day before trial, was overstated by $40,000 because it included four acres later sold. He produced no document showing which land was sold or how much of the price related to the home’s land, so the agreed value stood.Finally, the trial court valued the couple’s collectable cars at their insured values. Todd said he had over-insured them and offered his own lower estimates. The trial judge found the insurance figures more credible, calling them hard numbers, and noted that Todd had a reason to undervalue the cars in a divorce. Because that finding rested on a credibility judgment and supporting evidence, the appeals court deferred to it.How the equalisation payment shifted the split to 81.4 per cent for him and 18.6 per cent for herAn equalisation payment is a transfer from the spouse who holds more property to the other, evening out the final division. The couple’s assets totalled roughly $3.3 million, against nearly $900,000 in liabilities. Before the payment, the trial court’s allocation gave Todd a net $2,365,414 (95.6 per cent) and Julie $108,634 (4.4 per cent). After it, Todd received $2,013,968 and Julie $460,080.Todd argued the order grossly failed to do equity. He wanted the payment recalculated from only about $381,311 of remaining marital assets, after removing $2 million he called nonmarital. He did not propose a new figure.The judges found the outcome fair for several reasons. A short marriage makes a lopsided division more likely to be equitable. The trial court had also awarded all of Todd’s premarital property to him and reduced the payment so that it concentrated on sharing the growth in that property’s value.Julie’s contributions weighed heavily in the trial court’s findings. She helped with painting and cleaning, managed tenants and carried most of the household duties. She also decorated, furnished and landscaped the family home, and gave Todd emotional support. The panel accepted that some of the appreciation was fortuitous, such as investment account growth that did not come from either spouse’s transfers.Ability to pay also counted; even at the lowered income, Todd earns over four times what Julie does, and he was given 180 days to find the money. Todd, nearly twenty years older than Julie, was 60 at trial and had less time to rebuild retirement savings, but the trial court accounted for that by splitting growth in his investment account 65 per cent to him and 35 per cent to her. His claim to leave poorer than he entered found little support, and any decline stemmed largely from the investment loss. The decree was affirmed.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Bombay high court cancels bail granted to Sachin Waze in Antilia bomb scare and Mansukh Hiran murder case
articles.summary: MUMBAI: The Bombay high court on Thursday cancelled the bail granted by a special NIA trial court to Sachin Waze in the Antilia bomb scare and Mansukh
articles.body: MUMBAI: The Bombay high court on Thursday cancelled the bail granted by a special NIA trial court to Sachin Waze in the Antilia bomb scare and Mansukh Hiran murder case.A special bench of Justices Girish Kulkarni and Neela Gokhale, while pronouncing the judgment, said, "The order passed by special trial court on Sept 29 order in bail application (filed by Waze) is quashed and set aside and the appeal filed by NIA stands allowed." The reasoned order will follow.On October 16, the HC had concluded hearing an appeal filed by the National Investigation Agency (NIA) against the bail granted to the dismissed police officer by a special trial court and reserved the matter for orders. The HC bench had earlier stayed the bail order.On September 29, a special NIA trial court judge in Mumbai had directed Waze's release on bail, holding that no offence of a ‘terrorist act’ was prima facie evident under the anti-terror law, the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA).The NIA, however, argued in its appeal under the special law that the trial court had not considered the contents of the chargesheet in their proper perspective.Waze is the main accused in the February 25, 2021, Antilia bomb scare and Mansukh Hiran murder case. The car contained gelatin sticks and a threat note, which took the case into the political arena, Additional Solicitor General Anil Singh, appearing for the NIA, said.He stressed that threatening the country's richest family was intended to send a larger message through an act likely to threaten the security or economic security of the country or strike terror in the community.Waze was arrested on March 13, 2021, and has been behind bars since. His counsel, VM Thorat, cited his prolonged incarceration as one of the grounds for bail, besides the absence of detonators, which, he argued, meant the incident did not constitute a terror act and therefore did not attract the stringent UAPA provisions.He also argued that the trial could not begin until all forensic reports were available.For the NIA, Singh, however, argued that charges had been framed and the trial could begin soon. He also said, "It is not a private matter. articles.title: Could this be the last Bonfire Night for noisy fireworks?
articles.summary: About 20 million people enjoy fireworks at home every year, but some campaigners want quieter displays.
articles.body:
Bangers, rockets and screamers have long been part of Bonfire Night - but the traditional celebrations might sound a little different next year.

The government is currently considering reducing the noise limit for fireworks by 50% for those bought in shops for private use, after pressure from campaigners concerned about the impact on nervous animals and people with Post Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD).

Professionally organised displays would continue to have no maximum limit provided the noise level is not harmful to human health.

About 20 million people enjoy fireworks at home every year, according to industry figures.

Andy Hubble, of the British Fireworks Association (BFA), said displays had already been getting quieter and a balance must be struck to prevent a black market in noisy fireworks springing up.

The end of October sees the start of several celebrations traditionally marked by fireworks and bonfires, including Halloween on 31 October, Guy Fawkes Night on 5 November, and Diwali, which is on 8 November this year.

The government has said an outright ban on the public buying fireworks would not be proportionate.

But Business Minister Kate Dearden said her department was considering "reforms to fireworks legislation, focused on their key harms associated with their misuse - their noise, and contribution to antisocial behaviour – whilst still allowing individuals to enjoy fireworks safely and responsibly for the important community and cultural celebrations they play a part of."

It is already illegal to sell fireworks to under 18s, or to set fireworks off after 23:00, with exemptions for special occasions including Bonfire Night, Diwali, New Year's Eve and Chinese New Year.

But campaigners have raised concerns about the impact of loud bangs on nervous pets.

Dog owner Katherine Alderson, from Clacton-on-Sea, told BBC Breakfast: "It's a nightmare every single year.

"This year I've actually barricaded my bedroom window with numerous layers of insulation to try and keep out the noise of fireworks."

Asked whether reducing the bangs would take the fun out of fireworks, she said she believed displays "should be about the lights and colours" and suggested "a complete ban" on the sale of fireworks to the general public could be the solution.

But other campaigners say a ban is not needed, including Alan Friggieri, from the charity Combat Stress, which supports veterans with PTSD.

Giving evidence to MPs on the Commons' Business Committee, Friggieri said calls to their helpline jump at this time of year because loud bangs can trigger PTSD symptoms.

"Nothing quite sounds like an AK47 other than fireworks going off - it's that crackle," one veteran who had been shot multiple times had told him.

Friggieri said veterans need to be able to plan around key dates, but he said he was not calling for a ban, because his organisation understands the cultural importance of firework displays.

Calling for better enforcement of existing rules by police to stop antisocial behaviour, BFA vice chairman Hubble warned a ban in Ireland had seen a flourishing black market in firework sales.

"There is a real risk here that if we make fireworks quieter that there is still a demand then we could create an illegal market where fireworks are coming in through internet sales and white van sales," he told BBC Breakfast.

"At the moment we have a really well-regulated market where we have enforcers that know the products and can test them but as soon as these products go undercover then we lose that.

"We could actually create a louder and noisier environment because those are the sorts of fireworks that we're seeing coming in through illegal sales on the internet."

Asked whether it was true that displays were getting noisier, Hubble said: "No, no, it's a lot quieter than it used to be - we used to have bangers and air bombs and and screamer rockets that used to be on sale and they were withdrawn from sale."

The government is considering reducing the maximum noise limit from the current 120dB, equivalent toa thunderclap, to 110dB, which is equivalent to a car horn.

Hubble said a BFA assessment of firework sales shows a 50% noise reduction to 110 dB would impact up to 60% of firework sales to the general public.

Lowering levels to 90DB, equivalent to a lawnmower, as some campaigners want, would affect about 95% of fireworks.

"That's effectively a ban on consumer fireworks, not a modest reduction in noise," he said.

RSPCA advice for people with nervous pets:

Stay calm and show your pet that all is well

Put on music or the TV to help mask firework sounds

Close any windows and do what you can to block out both the noise and the flashes

Keep your environment secure: make sure your pet can't escape if there's a sudden noise

For dogs: let them pace around, if they're whining, barking or hiding, let them

Play with a toy if your pet wants to join in, but don't force them to play

Combat Stress advice for people with PTSD:

Use noise cancelling headphones to reduce the sound of explosions and blackout blinds to block out flashes of light

Use scented candles, diffusers or plug ins to make your home smell good and nothing like those you remember from deployments

Remind yourself you are safe, and focus on the present using breathing and grounding techniques, or with exercise

Ask friends and family to be with you on key dates like Bonfire Night

articles.title: Workers strike across France, hundreds of thousands expected to protest
articles.summary: Demonstrators are demanding an increase in the minimum wage and higher salaries for all workers, among other reforms.
articles.body:
Workers across France have gone on strike following calls by trade unions, with hundreds of thousands of people expected to take to the streets.

Protesters gathered across the country on Thursday, including in the capital, Paris, the southern cities of Marseille and Lyon, as well as in the western city of Nantes and Lille in the north.

Ahead of the demonstrations, President Emmanuel Macron convened a defence and security meeting on Wednesday to “ensure public order”.

France has seen regular protests since September, when students began demonstrating against poor conditions at public high schools. The rallies have since expanded to encompass a host of grievances linked to the rising cost of living.

Those striking on Thursday are demanding an increase in the minimum wage, higher salaries for all workers, tax reforms and better conditions in schools. Organisers said protests were expected in 260 cities and towns, with the Education Ministry expecting 16 percent of teachers nationwide to strike.

The protests come at a crucial time for France politically. The country is due to elect a new president in April next year, with incumbent Emmanuel Macron unable to run again because of a two-term limit. Polls suggest far-right candidate Marine Le Pen is the favourite to win, which would make her France’s first female president.

Reporting from Marseille, Al Jazeera’s Rebecca Collard said “these protests started in Paris with the student movement. In the last few weeks, we’ve seen them spread across the country and Marseille is one of the cities where we’ve seen some of the largest.”

Hugo, a history student attending a protest in Lille, told Al Jazeera that he was angry about the social situation in France.

“The workers are angry that wages are too low, life is getting more and more expensive and in the universities and high schools, we can feel the lack of public services. So there is a common anger in the country and that’s why I am here today. I’m angry about this social situation,” he said.

“There is money in the society but it’s in the hand of a small group of people and we have to fight to change the situation,” he added.

The Reuters news agency reported that riot police fired tear gas at a demonstration in Lyon.

Several European countries, including Germany and Portugal, have seen protests in recent weeks over declining living standards and a shortage of affordable housing.

France has faced criticism for its handling of the demonstrations, with several people making allegations of police violence.

Reuters reported that the upcoming G7 foreign ministers’ meeting ⁠has been moved from Marseille to Paris at the last minute, a move that follows six weeks ⁠of nationwide protests. Diplomats told Reuters the decision was “chaotic” and would harm France’s image.

articles.title: Melania Trump to host Russia and Ukraine representatives at the White House in a rare meeting
articles.summary: First lady Melania Trump will host representatives from Russia and Ukraine at the White House on Thursday, her latest diplomatic initiative after an unprecedented humanitarian ceasefire she helped broker between the warring sides.
articles.body: First lady Melania Trump will host representatives from Russia and Ukraine at the White House on Thursday, her latest diplomatic initiative after an unprecedented humanitarian ceasefire she helped broker between the warring sides. The meeting comes as the Trump administration pushes for progress in broader peace negotiations, with the United States set to lead renewed trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, next week. The losses suffered by Republicans in the midterm elections dealt a setback to President Donald Trump and his foreign policy, injecting yet more uncertainty into the American approach to the conflict. “This event represents an extraordinary moment in American history,” the White House said in a statement announcing Thursday’s meeting. It appears that this will be the first time both sides will meet face-to-face at the White House. It is unclear what exactly the gathering was designed to achieve and whether the president or any of his envoys would attend. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. President Vladimir Putin’s special envoy Kirill Dmitriev and human rights commissioner Yana Lantratova, who coordinated the humanitarian ceasefire on the Russian side, were expected to represent Russia at the gathering, according to the Kremlin. Ukraine has not officially confirmed who will attend the meeting from its side, but the head of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s ruling faction in parliament, David Arakhamia, will be part of the country’s delegation, his office told NBC News, signaling that attendees would be high-level officials. The gathering comes as Trump ramped up pressure on Kyiv and agreed on deals with the Kremlin in a bid to break a monthslong deadlock in negotiations to settle the war. Those efforts were boosted by the humanitarian truce, which started Oct. 27 and lasted six days, allowing for the evacuation of hundreds of people from Oleshky. The town in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region was home to some 2,000 remaining residents on the brink of starvation. Both sides held fire throughout the truce, making it the largest de-escalation effort since Russia’s full-scale invasion in early 2022. “This achievement marks an unprecedented diplomatic initiative by an American First Lady,” the White House said Tuesday of the ceasefire. Pope Leo XIV and some officials in Europe also lobbied heavily for the ceasefire in Oleshky. On Wednesday, Ukraine bestowed a state award on Melania Trump for “significant personal contribution to humanitarian support for Ukraine.” The Order of Princess Olga, 1st class is an honor for women who have made an outstanding contribution to the country. Ukraine has been reeling from the worst collapse in relations with Washington since the start of the war. Trump signed a deal to buy Russian diesel and waived new sanctions on Moscow last month, while Kyiv complained of gaps in U.S. intelligence sharing and the slowdown of tech billionaire Elon Musk’s Starlink service, crucial for Ukraine’s military and air defense. Ukraine has since said that both intelligence sharing and Starlink service have been restored, and that it was looking forward to resuming trilateral talks with the U.S. and Russia next week. “This will be a team-level format, and we count on the work in this format and our other diplomatic steps opening the way to a trilateral format at the leaders’ level,” Zelenskyy said Tuesday. “It is precisely such a format — at the leaders’ level — that can resolve the key issues in order to achieve a lasting peace and guaranteed security.” The meeting comes after Democrats captured full control of Congress in a striking repudiation of Trump’s agenda. Kremlin said it “sincerely hoped” that Trump would continue his “peace-building efforts” after the midterm elections. Ukraine offered no official response to the dramatic results, but some in the country expressed cautious optimism the Democratic surge would ease pressure from Washington. The negotiations to settle the war, led by Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner, have stalled over the key question of Ukraine’s eastern Donbas industrial region, which Putin wants to seize in its entirety. Ukraine still controls key stronghold cities in the Donbas and has refused to give up this land, arguing Putin may be eyeing not just a public relations success but a powerful launchpad for future invasion attempts.

articles.title: Man catches thief with Apple AirTag hidden in stone
articles.summary: Matt Smith hid the tracker inside a piece of stone and police followed the trail to the culprit's house.
articles.body:
A thief who was stealing a wall piece by piece was caught when a man put a tracking device in one of the stones.

Matt Smith said people living near Rufford Old Hall in Lancashire, "were getting a bit miffed" with stones being taken from the 300-year-old boundary wall.

So he put an Apple AirTag - a coin-sized tracking device people attack to keys or wallets in case they lose them - inside one of the stone.

Police followed the trail to an address in Wigan, and earlier this month, a man pleaded guilty at Wigan Magistrates' Court to two counts of theft and one count of handling stolen goods.

Last October, about 30 stones went missing from a half-mile-long stretch of road which connects Holmeswood and Rufford.

"We looked at installing some CCTV, but it costs and with the wall being attacked at random places at random times, in a half mile stretch of wall, it was going to be hard to cover that area," Smith, a parish councillor, told BBC Radio Lancashire.

He added: "So we put some lovely 'smile you're on camera' signs up and unfortunately that didn't deter them.

"So I devised a plan and spoke with the owners.

"We'd noticed it was the smaller of the stones that were being taken, so we put a tracking device in what we thought would maybe be the next stone to be taken.

"So there was a bit of guesswork involved."

Matt said he "lifted a couple of the smaller coping stones off, core drilled into the bottom of those and placed in an Apple AirTag, patched up the core, ground it up, put a bit of resin in" and placed it back on the wall.

"Lo and behold, four weeks later my phone started to ping with the tracking device on the move to an address in Winstanley in Wigan," he said.

He contacted the police, who went to the address and made an arrest.

The coping stones were later returned and the "extremely grateful" residents rebuilt the wall.

Last month, Craig Barker, 41, from Wigan, pleaded guilty to theft and handling stolen goods and was given a 12-month sentence, suspended for 22 months.

PC Sean Dalby, of the South Rural Task Force, said: "This case highlights the strong relationships we have developed with our communities and demonstrates the effectiveness of working together to tackle rural and heritage crime.

"I would like to thank the local residents for their support throughout the investigation, as well as those who gave their time to rebuild the wall free of charge."
