articles.title: Joint List says it will back Eisenkot to form Israel’s next government
articles.summary: Arab-led parties won a record 19 seats in Israel’s 120-seat parliament in last week’s general election.
articles.body:
The Joint List alliance of Arab-led parties says it will back Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot to form a new government after last week’s election.

“The Joint List announced today, Thursday, that it will inform the President of the State, Isaac Herzog, this evening of its decision to recommend that Gadi Eisenkot be tasked with forming the government,” the alliance said in a statement.

Arab-led parties won a record 19 seats in Israel’s 120-seat parliament in last week’s general election, a result that could give them significant influence over the formation of the next government.

Once the Joint List’s 11 lawmakers formally submit their recommendation, Eisenkot is expected to have the backing of 67 lawmakers, exceeding the 61-seat majority threshold in the Knesset.

Earlier, Ra’am, an Arab-led party with eight seats, said it would also recommend Eisenkot.

Meanwhile, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc with 53 seats may not yield 53 endorsements, as Degel HaTorah, which holds four of United Torah Judaism’s seven seats, said it would recommend neither candidate.

The ultra-Orthodox faction broke with Netanyahu over his coalition’s failure to pass legislation exempting Haredi men from military service, The Times of Israel reported.

Netanyahu has also claimed repeatedly and without evidence that Arab parties committed fraud during the elections with foreign backing.

The prime minister and his Likud party have cited a handful of cases, including the arrests of three political activists who allegedly bribed voters before polls opened. They are suspected of connections with the Ra’am party, although the party denies any involvement.

Netanyahu and Likud also suggested that the opposition bloc joining with Arab-led parties would be treasonous. In a statement after the vote, Likud warned that Zionist parties cooperating with the Arab bloc would be “dangerous to Israel”.

Israel’s Central Elections Committee certified the results of the election on Wednesday after finding no evidence of fraud.

Israel’s President Isaac Herzog has also accepted the results and begun consultations with party leaders on whom to task with forming the next government.

He also backed investigating suspected interference but warned against smearing voters who are Palestinian citizens of Israel, saying he had “great respect” for the country’s Palestinian minority, which makes up about 20 percent of the population.

“I condemn the coarseness and racist expressions that we have heard recently,” he said.

On Wednesday, the president said he had met representatives of the Religious Zionism and Zehut, Shas and Yisrael Beytenu factions.

In a post on X, Herzog said he “received their recommendations regarding the identity of the Knesset member upon whom the task of forming the government should be assigned”.

Herzog added that talks would also continue on Thursday.

Once the consultations end, Herzog will choose the candidate he considers best placed to assemble a coalition, almost certainly Netanyahu or Eisenkot. He has several days to announce his decision, after which the nominee will have 28 days to form a government, with a possible 14-day extension.

If neither man succeeds, Israel would hold another election early next year.

articles.body: LONDON — British comedian and actor Russell Brand has been found guilty of rape and sexual assault in a London court on Thursday. Brand, ⁠once ‌one of Britain’s most high-profile ‌broadcasters and the ‌former husband of ⁠singer Katy Perry, had denied the accusations, saying the incidents ‌had either ​been ‌consensual, reinvented ⁠or re-imagined. Brand, 51, was accused of three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of attempted indecent assault. Ultimately he was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. He ⁠was acquitted of ⁠the other charges. He had pleaded not guilty to all counts and consistently denied all of the allegations. The judge, Justice Joel Bennathan, told Brand in court that the consequence of the verdicts is a “significant custodial term” and said he would have to remain in prison until he is formally sentenced on Monday. “You’ve been convicted of a number of offenses including rape,” Bennathan said, adding that Brand inevitably faced a “significant” prison sentence. The maximum sentence for rape is life imprisonment and 10 years for one count of sexual assault, according to Britain’s Sentencing Council. The accusations date back to Brand’s rise as a stand-up comedian and risqué presenter on British television. He also had a prominent radio show on the BBC and authored several best-selling biographies where he detailed his addictions to drugs and alcohol. At the height of his fame, Brand featured in several Hollywood movies including: “Forgetting Sarah Marshall” and “Get Him to the Greek.” His fame stateside was cemented when he briefly wed pop star Katy Perry in a lavish ceremony in India in 2010. The couple divorced in 2012. In recent years, Brand has moved away from mainstream media, relocated to Florida and built a large online following with videos that discuss U.S. politics, wellness, conspiracy theories and his newfound Christian faith. The four-week trial at Southwark Crown Court in London saw prosecutors label Brand “ruthless.” Prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones told jurors that Brand at the time had an “indiscriminate and voracious” desire for sexual contact, and that “women were simply a means to an end.” The prosecutor described Brand as “calculating, he was manipulative. And, the prosecution say, he was a sexual predator.” Brand was found guilty of raping one woman in 2009. She said he anally raped her at his home after she met him at one of his shows. He was also found guilty of sexually assaulting a woman whose breasts he grabbed at a party in 2004 and another woman who said he had kissed and groped her at a London radio station in 2004 or 2005. A third guilty verdict was delivered for the sexual assault of a woman who testified that he pressed his face into her groin during the recording of an advertisement in 2009. Prosecutors said the women do not know one another and separately went to police after a TV documentary was broadcast in Britain in 2023. His appearances outside the court, holding hands with his wife and flanked by security guards, made daily headlines in the British press. Last week, Brand took the stand and said the claims had made a “devastating” impact on his life, leaving him without a single friend or colleague who could testify on his behalf. “My entire life has been consumed by these events,” he said inside court, adding later that dealing with the “traumatic” allegations had come “at the expense of my marriage, my children and health.” He admitted in court to being sex obsessed as a young and famous man. “I have been persuasive, seductive, begging and flirting, and have dedicated a ​lot of my life to what seems now beyond reckless philandering and idiocy,” he told the court as he gave evidence last Wednesday. “I was in a position of fame. As I became more successful and famous I was ​very comfortable allowing that to facilitate sexual access, which I agree was wrong,” he added. Brand also told the court: “Consent is fundamental, essential, necessary and indeed more important than sex itself.” Brand’s wife, Laura Gallacher, also made headlines when she testified last week, stating that he was a “caring, kind and a wonderful father.” The couple married in 2017 and have three young children. Brand and his wife have been posting videos online where they analyze bible verses together and discuss their broad experiences of the trial. When the trial first got underway last month, Brand told a scrum of photographers and journalists that he felt “blessed.” He said he was “hopeful that this process will lead to good outcomes for everybody involved.” He added, “that’s my prayer.” In a statement after the verdict, Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy from London’s Metropolitan Police said Brand had “used his influence, status and fame to exploit and sexually offend against women.” “As his profile grew, so too did his sense of entitlement,” he said. Praising the victims for their “extraordinary courage,” he added: “Despite intense media and public scrutiny, they relived deeply personal and traumatic experiences and placed their trust in us. Without their bravery, this outcome would not have been possible.” If you or someone you know has been sexually assaulted, call the National Sexual Assault Hotline at 1-800-656-4673. The hotline, run by the Rape, Abuse, & Incest National Network (RAINN), can put you in contact with your local rape crisis center. articles.summary: British comedian was convicted by jury at London court of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.
articles.body:
British comedian and actor Russell Brand has been found guilty of rape and sexual assault by a London court and could face a lengthy prison sentence.

A jury at London’s Southwark Crown Court on Thursday convicted the 51-year-old of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. He was acquitted of two other rape charges and one count of attempted indecent assault.

Brand, who was one of the most prominent broadcasters in Britain and the former husband of American pop star Katy Perry, had denied the allegations. He maintained that the encounters were consensual or that the allegations had been fabricated.

Prosecutors described Brand, who starred in the films Get Him to the Greek and Arthur, as a “ruthless” sexual predator.

Judge Joel Bennathan said Brand would be sentenced on Monday and faced a lengthy prison term. Brand was taken into custody following the verdict.

Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy of London’s Metropolitan Police said the conviction was “a testament to the extraordinary courage, resilience and determination of the women who came forward and reported what happened to them”.

“Brand used his influence, status and fame to exploit and sexually offend against women,” Furphy said.

“As his profile grew, so too did his sense of entitlement.”

Prosecutors said the charges, which covered incidents between 1999 and 2009, spanned the years in which Brand rose from performing stand-up comedy in small venues to becoming a television presenter and Hollywood film star.

The court heard testimony from six complainants, all of whom are entitled to lifelong anonymity. None of the women knew each other, but all came forward to the police following a television documentary and press reports in 2023 containing anonymous allegations against Brand by other women.

The most graphic evidence related to the rape for which he was convicted took place in 2009, involving a victim who had met Brand after a gig where she had engaged in a sexual encounter in his dressing room.

She recounted how days later she had gone to his home, where during consensual sex, he had anally raped her. Afterwards, he had told her to clean up the blood and mess, she said.

Brand was also convicted of sexually assaulting a woman at a London bar in 2004. The woman told the court he approached her at a party and grabbed her breasts.

articles.title: US 2026 Midterms | Vivek Ramaswamy and Zohran Mamdani: A tale of two Indian-Americans
articles.summary: Explore the contrasting political paths of Vivek Ramaswamy and Zohran Mamdani during the 2026 midterms, highlighting their backgrounds, ideologies and election outcomes.
articles.body: One of the most famous opening lines in literature comes from Charles Dickens’ A Tale of Two Cities: “It was the best of times, it was the worst of times, it was the age of wisdom, it was the age of foolishness, it was the epoch of belief, it was the epoch of incredulity, it was the season of Light, it was the season of Darkness, it was the spring of hope, it was the winter of despair, we had everything before us, we had nothing before us, we were all going direct to Heaven, we were all going direct the other way—in short, the period was so far like the present period, that some of its noisiest authorities insisted on its being received, for good or for evil, in the superlative degree of comparison only.”And that’s as apt a description as one can have for Republicans and Democrats after the midterms. For Dems, it’s the best of times, the age of wisdom has returned and it’s the season of light. For the MAGA-cannibalised GOP, it’s the worst of times, a winter of despair. It’s the happiest Dems – and their global surrogates across the world – have been since a man with the middle name Hussein declared “Yes We Can”. For Republicans, it’s the most devastating loss in decades, with Kansas waving goodbye for the first time since 1932 while the Texas Senate seat flipped after 38 years.In the Lone Star State – the online memes have already labelled it the Lone Saar State – the Republicans’ bilious anti-Indian rhetoric ensured that the Texas House would now have a Pooja in its midst, a befitting reply to the slogan: “Don’t Pooja my Texas.”Much like the 2024 US election, which was billed as an internecine desi fight thanks to Kamala Harris’ Tamil Brahmin ancestry and Usha Vance’s Telugu roots, Indian-American representation in the midterms was off the charts.Now, just to be clear, Indian-Americans make up roughly 1.5% of the US population and 1% of its eligible electorate, and even Texas – where Bo French’s anti-India rant will live on in history as the most famous political upheaval since a Gujarati man was asked to deboard a train in South Africa for being brown – has an Indian population of only 2%, with just 1% being voters.Now, in both cases, we flirt with what logicians call post hoc ergo propter hoc, but we digress.While Trump made historic gains among numerous groups in Texas (and the US) in 2024, including Indian-Americans, those gains were largely eroded by the time the midterms came around. And all elections can always be summed up by one simple line from Bill Clinton’s former adviser Jim Carville: “It’s the economy, stupid.”But from an Indian-American lens, and from a broader Republican vs Democrat debate, the midterms can be viewed through the journeys of two Indian-American politicians: one who was on the ballot during the midterms and one who wasn’t.A Tale of Two Indian-AmericansNow, New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Ohio's losing gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy are like chalk and cheese, and before they got into politics, the average desi family would happily adopt Ramaswamy and be reluctant to even acknowledge Mamdani as a cousin.Mamdani was a rapper who didn’t get into Columbia – despite claiming to be African-American as well as Asian-American – while Ramaswamy was a high-school valedictorian who got into Ivy League schools and sold his company for a billion dollars.But while what is sauce for the goose might be sauce for the gander in real life, in politics, chalk can morph into cheese.Today, Mamdani is one of the three desi mayors of what can be called the Dard-E-Disco cities (New York, LA, London, Paris, San Francisco), along with Sadiq Khan (London) and Nithya Raman (LA), while Ramaswamy is a losing gubernatorial candidate in Ohio, a contest that he looked bang on to win before Trump went full Trump.Mamdani, in particular, might have thrilled his teachers with his academic brilliance, but he has a certain je ne sais quoi about him as a politician that can warm the cockles of his harshest critic. Just ask Trump, who has had a stronger man crush on Mamdani than he has had on any Republican of note.On the other hand, there’s a similar negative je ne sais quoi about Ramaswamy, aptly summed up by Indian-American comedian Nimesh Patel in a 2023 stand-up act in which he says all Indians know a guy like Ramaswamy, who “lucked into a bunch of money” and now thinks he is – one is paraphrasing here to keep it publication-friendly – the biggest stick on the planet.And both their political trajectories make for interesting reading.To understand these trajectories, however, we must first understand the two very different versions of postcolonial Indian privilege that these men inherited.Mamdani is the quintessential lovechild of India's liberal, cosmopolitan and intellectual elite. His mother, Mira Nair, grew up in the household of an IAS officer in post-Independence India, studied at Delhi University and Harvard. Her films might not pack theatres to the rafters in India, but their exploration of migration, identity and class makes people who go to art festivals that hand out laurel wreaths feel smug about themselves.His father, Mahmood Mamdani, was born in Bombay, grew up in Uganda, was expelled under Idi Amin and went on to become one of the world's foremost scholars of colonialism, citizenship and political identity. A Harvard PhD and Columbia professor, Mahmood spent much of his academic career interrogating the structures of power that colonialism had left behind.Ergo, Mamdani grew up in a house where Edward Said and Rashid Khalidi dropped in as dinner guests, where one assumes discussions about colonialism, imperialism and identity were as commonplace as discussions of IIT preparations are in Indian middle-class households. One could argue that even though Mamdani couldn't get into Columbia, Columbia came home to him.Ramaswamy inherited a different version of the Indian Dream though he too was a fan of rapping.Born in Cincinnati to Tamil-speaking Palakkad Iyer Brahmin parents, Ramaswamy was raised by an engineer who became a patent lawyer at General Electric and a mother who worked as a geriatric psychiatrist. His parents belonged to that extraordinary generation of highly educated Indian professionals who migrated to America and discovered that their qualifications, discipline and willingness to work extraordinarily hard could propel them into the upper reaches of American society.And Ramaswamy followed the script almost perfectly: valedictorian, Harvard, Yale Law School, hedge funds, biotechnology and eventually selling his company for a cool billion dollars before deciding to become America’s corporate mascot against wokeism and social justice. His infamous Boxing Day rant in 2024 was practically an Indian parent-teacher meeting masquerading as an American political manifesto.As the ensuing MAGA civil war demonstrated, Americans weren't particularly interested in being told by a billionaire of Indian origin that they should have spent less time watching sitcoms and more time solving quadratic equations.Therein lies the split between the two: one came from the intellectual tradition of questioning inequality while being steeped in social capital, while the other came from a professional tradition that believes excellence, discipline and individual achievement can trump any system.Products of PrivilegeBoth are products of privilege.Of course, both are products of privilege, but the fascinating contrast saw Mamdani become a socialist insurgent against the economic establishment while Ramaswamy became the capitalist insurgent looking to restore the meritocratic American Dream that made his extraordinary ascent possible.But what makes the contrast fascinating is how differently they translated those inheritances into American politics.Now, an asinine argument would be to boil down their contrasting political fortunes to their respective religions, particularly when both men have been rather open about their faith, albeit in very different ways.Ramaswamy, while proudly identifying as Hindu, has often presented his faith in a language that makes it sound like a crypto-Christian religion, emphasising one true God and the Judeo-Christian values supposedly underpinning American civilisation. His attempts to make Hinduism palatable to evangelical conservatives have sometimes resembled a theological translation exercise.Mamdani, meanwhile, has been unabashedly Muslim, whether campaigning among New York's diverse communities or turning up for Eid prayers in an Arsenal-themed kurta, demonstrating that one could combine religious devotion, cultural identity and the considerably more serious business of supporting a football club.But the idea that Mamdani succeeded because he was Muslim while Ramaswamy lost because he was Hindu would be particularly asinine.The Carnegie survey of Indian-Americans found that enthusiasm for Mamdani's victory was driven far more by his ideology than his religious identity. Neither the New York mayoral election nor the Ohio gubernatorial contest was a referendum on theological compatibility.Culture wars might dominate television studios and political podcasts, not to mention the more deranged corners of Twitter, but they don’t make the weekly grocery bill disappear.Mamdani's 2025 mayoral campaign demonstrated that even a self-declared socialist could win over voters in the capital of global capitalism by addressing their most immediate concerns and, in doing so, beat a former governor who enjoyed considerable establishment backing.His campaign had a distinctly modern vocabulary. The videos were funny, the slogans memorable and the use of social media imaginative. Mamdani spoke to immigrant communities in their languages – even though native Bengali speakers would wonder if what he was saying was even Bengali – but none of that distracted from his promise to make New York affordable.And this defeat came when the Democrats were at their lowest ebb, reeling from a Trump victory that made believing in blue seem like a pipe dream.And his subsequent political impact demonstrated why his victory mattered far beyond the five boroughs. Many of Mamdani’s endorsements resulted in victories in the midterms.In the communication war that was comfortably being won by Republicans, Mamdani showed how to counter Trump’s political communication while demonstrating that he had mastered the art of the deal better than any Republican.Since Obama's departure, the Democrats had often seemed caught between competing impulses: appealing to traditional working-class voters, satisfying their increasingly progressive activist base, reassuring wealthy donors and defending institutions that large sections of the electorate no longer trusted.Mamdani offered a way of resolving some of those contradictions, at least electorally.In simple words, it showed Democrats they could offer voters an alternative rather than harping on about how terrible the Republicans were. And those same instincts made him the only Democrat who could cajole offerings out of Trump with fake newspaper headings and handshakes.Meanwhile, Ramaswamy was one of the breakout stars of the 2024 Republican presidential primaries, becoming Trump’s surrogate: a Hindu billionaire whose most enthusiastic supporters often associated American identity with Christianity.He eventually abandoned his presidential ambitions, endorsed Trump and was selected alongside Elon Musk to lead the proposed Department of Government Efficiency.Then came the Boxing Day rant, the MAGA civil war over H-1B visas and his departure from DOGE.The official explanation was that he was leaving to pursue the Ohio governorship. Other reports suggested that his remarks about American culture, along with his differences with Musk and other figures in Trump's orbit, had made his position increasingly untenable.But in February 2025, the move to Ohio looked like a rather clever escape plan.Ramaswamy was running in a state Trump had won by more than 11 percentage points in 2024. He had Trump's endorsement, the support of influential Republican figures and the financial resources to build a formidable statewide organisation.His campaign was flush with funds, and he appeared to be saying and doing all the right things. He promised lower costs, bigger paycheques, world-class schools, cheaper energy and reduced taxes. His economic programme was substantially different from Mamdani's. Rather than expanding state intervention, he wanted to reduce taxation, deregulate economic activity and make Ohio a more attractive destination for investment and employment.In theory, it was a perfectly plausible political proposition in a state that had supported Trump three times and where many voters had embraced the Republican promise of economic revival.For much of 2025, Ramaswamy appeared well positioned to win. But as the ship that was Trump’s second presidency sank – vacillating from one madcap moment to another while taking the American and global economies down with it – Ramaswamy appeared stuck to the hull.Soon, Republicans who had sworn their fealty couldn’t dislodge themselves quickly enough. And as his Catch-22 problem with MAGA became increasingly apparent, his campaign struggled to reconcile the need to energise Trump's base with the equally important task of winning over moderate voters.Many of these problems were beyond his control: hostility towards Indians, vile anti-immigrant rhetoric and the cost of living hitting almost everyone in America and, thanks to the interconnected global economy, almost everyone across the globe.Of course, the final nail in his coffin was of his own making: the vile ad in which his campaign wheeled out the estranged mother of his opponent Amy Acton to bring up Acton's childhood sexual abuse by her stepfather. It was the kind of low that would make Trump think twice, though he did back the ad.The advertisement provoked outrage across party lines, and an internal Republican poll reported by Axios found Acton’s lead increasing from two points to eight points after the ad began circulating. For the better part of a year and more, Ramaswamy had talked about opportunity and excellence but spent the final weeks attempting to destroy his opponent’s personal credibility in a Trumpian move that didn’t work at all.The two campaigns, and the parties they came to symbolise, had made very different choices. Mamdani persuaded people to imagine how their lives might improve. Ramaswamy, after months of promising excellence, ended by asking voters to think the worst of his opponent.Dickens wrote of the spring of hope and the winter of despair as two seasons belonging to the same age. The American electorate witnessed both in November 2026. Mamdani chose hope. Ramaswamy chose despair. And the results suggested which had proved more persuasive. Of course, politics is the art of the possible, and nothing is ever final. No one watching Trump's triumphant return at the end of 2024 could have imagined that, barely two years later, the Democrats would see the blue moon rising quite like this. But then, as Dickens understood, the best of times and the worst of times have an inconvenient habit of changing places.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Protests erupt across France after left-wing groups call for mobilization
articles.summary: An estimated 270,000 people joined nationwide strikes and protests across France on Thursday, putting pressure on President Emmanuel Macron's government.
articles.body: France deployed 70,000 police officers Thursday as tens of thousands of people took to the streets for nationwide strikes and protests after left-wing groups called for a mobilization. In Paris, the Eiffel Tower was closed; in Lyon, French riot police fired tear gas and charged a group of protesters; and near Toulouse, a high school was set on fire, according to Reuters. "We need to turn up in big numbers on the streets today," the news agency quoted the head of the left-wing CGT union Sophie Binet as saying. The demonstrations come after France was rocked by violent protests in October, which outgoing French President Emmanuel Macron blamed on "ultra-left groups whose aim is to bring down the Republic." FRANCE'S MACRON BLAMES PROTESTS ON 'ULTRA-LEFT GROUPS WHOSE AIM IS TO BRING DOWN THE REPUBLIC' An official close to Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said that by early Thursday, around 270,000 people had joined the union action in 180 rallies outside the capital. About a third of France’s high schools were closed or unable to operate, some because of student blockades and others because teachers were on strike, The Associated Press reported. Nuñez said the 70,000 police officers being deployed are backed by armored vehicles, drones and helicopters. Authorities in the western region of Brittany also said "masked individuals" tried to block roads in Rennes, while some committed "serious acts of violence," including throwing steel balls at police. AMERICANS WARNED OF VIOLENT PROTESTS AS MAJOR TOURIST DESTINATION FACES SHUTDOWN THREAT France’s main unions warned that the country is on the brink of recession and that layoff plans are multiplying. "Fuel, food products, rent, gas, electricity... everything’s going up except wages and pensions," they said in a joint statement, according to The Associated Press. The U.S. Embassy had issued an urgent security alert for Americans in France ahead of the demonstrations, warning travelers to brace for severe disruptions, sudden curfews and the potential for violence. The rallies come as the campaign to succeed Macron as president next May heats up, with political parties seeking to capitalize on the movement. articles.title: 6 people dead, others hospitalized after fire tears through Brooklyn home
articles.summary: Six people are dead following a tragic and destructive fire that quickly tore through a Brooklyn apartment in the middle of the night, FDNY officials said Thursday morning.
articles.body: Six people are dead following a tragic and destructive fire that quickly tore through a Brooklyn apartment in the middle of the night, FDNY officials said Thursday morning. The first 911 calls were made shortly after 1:30 a.m. for a fire in Sunset Park on 58th Street between 6th and 7th avenues. Responding firefighters found a two-story residential building engulfed in flames. Video captured giant flames flowing out of second-story windows and the loud pop of breaking glass . Neighbors were held back for the threat of black smoke and possible extension of the fire to buildings on either side. More than 200 firefighters responded to the block. Roughly an hour after the first call, firefighters were able to extinguish the deadly inferno. Additional video captured firefighters performing CPR on a victim laying on a stretcher outside. The FDNY said hazmat officials were called to the home for the presence of a lithium-ion battery. The battery has not yet been identified as the cause of the fire. The city’s medical examiner has been at the house all morning. In addition to the six people who lost their lives, four other civilians and three firefighters were injured. Officials said all six people who died were adults. No other information about them was immediately released. Mayor Zohran Mamdani offered condolences and said the fire was still under investigation. “This is an unimaginable loss, and we grieve alongside every loved one and neighbor and pray for the recovery of those injured,” Mamdani said in a statement on social media. “I am grateful for the FDNY’s swift response. Our administration is relocating displaced New Yorkers to safe housing and connecting them to long-term support and resources. The cause of the fire is still under investigation.”

articles.title: Clashes erupt in France as ‘Black Thursday’ protests sweep the nation
articles.summary: Riot police clashed with protesters in Lyon on Thursday as a nationwide public sector strike tapped into growing anger over deteriorating services and the rising cost of living.
articles.body: PARIS — Riot police clashed with protesters in Lyon on Thursday as a nationwide public sector strike tapped into growing anger over deteriorating services and the rising cost of living. Paris’ iconic Eiffel Tower was closed because of the strike. Officers clad in black helmets and protective clothing charged at crowds in Lyon after the demonstrations against rising living costs and in support of the high school protest movement turned violent and fires were set in the streets. Water cannons were also deployed. Some of the protesters wore gas masks and safety glasses as a precaution against tear gas. Images from Paris showed students and other protesters facing off against riot police. Police were “keeping the situation under control, but it remains tense,” the French Interior Ministry said in a statement at 1 p.m. local time (7 a.m. ET). “Several violent acts have been committed as part of the high school student movement,” the statement said. After fireworks were fired at a school near the southern city of Toulouse, a fire broke out “that burned the student services office,” it added. In the city of Rennes in northwest France, metal pétanque balls were thrown at officers, the statement said, adding that police had been pelted with other projectiles in the cities of Pau and Orleans. Around 250 rallies against rising living costs had been planned in cities and towns across the country and hundreds of thousands of people would likely turn out, unions said before the events kicked off. France’s main unions, including the CGT and CNT representing public and private sector workers, and the UNEF, representing students, warned the government of President Emmanuel Macron’s that the country was on the brink or recession. “Everything is going up except wages and pensions,” they said in a joint statement. “Anger is immense.” “The situation in this country is fragile. The pressing social and environmental challenges must be addressed without delay,” the statement added. The movement grew from a student protest over staff shortages at the Antoine de Saint-Exupéry High School in Créteil, a southeastern suburb of Paris. Videos of the blockade spread on social media, and soon protests expanded to high schools across the nation. As the movement grew, the list of grievances expanded beyond the failings of the public school system to encompass broader economic, political and social dissatisfaction. Soon, university students, teachers, parents and politicians also joined. Hundreds of thousands of protesters have since taken to the streets as the demonstrations expanded, with participants holding signs criticizing the far-right National Rally party and warning of the risks of climate change and artificial intelligence. A multitude of Palestinian flags have also been seen. Macron, who will leave office in May, convened a defense ‌and security meeting Wednesday ahead of the protests. Later, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said that 70,000 police officers would be deployed Thursday, backed by armored vehicles, drones and helicopters. Police have previously been criticized for injuring protesters with heavy-handed tactics. Last month, a 15-year-old was maimed by a sting ball grenade fired by police and a 14-year-old suffered a jaw fracture in a similar incident. Several other have also suffered life-changing injuries and a 59-year-old man, identified as Christophe M, died Oct. 17 of “a critical cardio-respiratory failing” after leaving Paris’ Place de la République which had been tear-gassed be police. An investigation into his death is ongoing. Zacharie Petit reported from Paris and Henry Austin from London.

articles.title: Cops return to New Jersey mother's home months after she was found stabbed and husband called 911
articles.summary: Police returned with at least 15 vehicles to Brooke Hanlon's Chester, New Jersey, home weeks after her autopsy ruled the stabbing a homicide.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: CHESTER, N.J. — Police returned Wednesday to the home where New Jersey mother Brooke Hanlon was found stabbed to death nearly five months ago. Neighbors of Brooke Hanlon told Fox News Digital that at least 15 law-enforcement vehicles were on scene and remained at the residence on Pottersville Road in Chester, New Jersey, until around 11 p.m. Her husband, Conor Hanlon, was seen speaking with police on Wednesday afternoon, her neighbors said. Conor Hanlon has denied any involvement in her death. No arrests have been made in the case. NJ MOM’S MURDER SHROUDED IN SECRECY AS PI SAYS ‘NEVER SEEN ANYTHING LIKE THIS’ BEHIND-CLOSED-DOORS CASE The Morris County Prosecutor's Office in New Jersey told Fox News Digital it has no updates regarding the investigation into Hanlon's death. She leaves behind a 1-year-old daughter. Investigators' return comes weeks after officials released Hanlon's autopsy, which ruled her death a homicide caused by "sharp force injuries." The autopsy confirms what Morris County Prosecutor's Office released in June. NJ HUSBAND BEGS FOR CPR HELP IN 911 CALL AFTER WIFE FOUND DEAD WITH STAB WOUNDS: AUDIO According to a 911 call obtained by Fox News Digital, Hanlon's husband was the first to discover her unresponsive. During the call, he told the operator, "There's a laceration" on his wife's body while the operator was walking him through how to perform CPR on her. LISTEN: 911 call reveals Brooke Hanlon’s husband frantically calling after discovering stab wounds SEND US A TIP "I just found my wife (inaudible) CPR, I need CPR instructions," Conor Hanlon can be heard saying on the 911 call. SLAIN NJ MOM BROOKE HANLON’S HUSBAND MAKES WEEKLY VISITS TO HOME, NEIGHBORS SAY "I need you here. I need you here immediately," he said. LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST Months after the mother was found dead, neighbors told Fox News Digital that Conor Hanlon has frequently returned to his home and spends nights there. Before that, he had been dividing his time between Chester and the Boston area, where his family is originally from. articles.title: 3 people have been injured in a shooting at an Iowa post office
articles.summary: DES MOINES, Iowa — A suspect was in custody in Des Moines, Iowa, Thursday after two people were shot at the city’s main post office and a third was injured trying to escape, authorities said.
articles.body: DES MOINES, Iowa — A suspect was in custody in Des Moines, Iowa, Thursday after two people were shot at the city’s main post office and a third was injured trying to escape, authorities said. None of the injuries were believed to be life-threatening, police said. “They’re all at the hospital, they are being cared for right now,” Sgt. Paul Parizek said of the victims. Parizek said officers responded within three minutes. The shooting happened on the second floor of the post office and reports started coming in of shots fired around 9:10 a.m. local time. The main post office is just north of downtown Des Moines and across the street from one of the city’s main hospitals. The building is a four-story regional sorting facility with a walk-in service counter accessible to the public. The Associated Press has several phone calls out seeking more information. Gov. Kim Reynolds said she’s in contact with the Department of Public Safety regarding the shooting. “The suspected shooter is in custody and the investigation is ongoing,” she posted online. “We are monitoring the situation and our prayers are with everyone involved. Grateful for the immediate response by law enforcement.” Des Moines Public Schools said that after being notified by police at 9:20 a.m. of the shooting at the post office, the district’s nearby elementary school, welcome center and nutrition center went into a secure status, meaning no one was allowed in or out of the buildings. The district said the secure status was lifted after police notified them at 10 a.m. that a suspect was in custody.
